procedural_history.originating_court: State of Gujarat under Section 3(1) of COFEPOSA
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention dated July 1, 1982, issued by the State Government under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA, served on the petitioner on July 2, 1982.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the detention order. The Supreme Court allowed the petition and quashed the detention order, directing the petitioner's release.

directions: The continued detention of the petitioner is quashed.
The petitioner is directed to be released forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure of the detaining authority to furnish copies of statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention, upon demand by the detenu, violates the constitutional mandate of Article 22(5) and vitiates the continued detention.

facts: The detenu was served with grounds of detention, but the supporting documents and statements were in languages he did not understand (English, Hindi, Gujarati).
Urdu translations of these documents, which the detenu understood, were not supplied within the normal period of 5 days.
The supply of these translations was delayed for up to 13 days, and even then, not all documents were translated.
The detaining authority failed to communicate any exceptional circumstances or recorded reasons that would justify this delay.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution, read with Section 3(3) of the COFEPOSA Act, grants a detenu the right to be informed of the grounds for detention and the right to make an effective representation against it.

To make the right of representation meaningful, the detaining authority has a constitutional duty to furnish the detenu with copies of all documents, statements, and other materials relied upon in the grounds of detention.
These materials must be supplied in a script or language that the detenu understands.
This must be done along with the grounds of detention or, at the latest, within five days, unless exceptional circumstances (which must be recorded in writing) justify a delay of up to 15 days.
application: The Court reasoned that the right to make a representation is the core constitutional safeguard, and it cannot be "meaningfully exercised" unless the detenu has access to the very materials that influenced the detaining authority's decision.
Merely providing the grounds of detention is insufficient; the underlying documents are essential for the detenu to effectively challenge the basis of the detention.

The Court held that the duty to supply these documents is mandatory. The failure to provide them in a language the detenu could understand within the prescribed time frame, without a valid and recorded justification for the delay, constituted a direct breach of the constitutional mandate.
This failure deprived the detenu of the opportunity to make an effective representation against his detention.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure of the detaining authority to furnish copies of the documents and statements relied upon in the grounds of detention, in a language understood by the detenu and within the prescribed time, violates the constitutional safeguard provided under Article 22(5). This violation vitiates the detention order and makes the continued detention illegal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure of the detaining authority to furnish copies of statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention, upon demand by the detenu, violates the constitutional mandate of Article 22(5) and vitiates the continued detention.
appellant_arguments: The failure to supply Urdu translations of documents and statements relied upon by the detaining authority prevented the detenu from making an effective representation against his detention.

The detenu is a Pakistani national whose mother tongue is Urdu, and his claim that he only knows Urdu cannot be dismissed, especially since a previous detention order was revoked for the same reason (failure to supply Urdu translations).
The right to receive copies of all relied-upon documents is a necessary implication of the constitutional right to make a representation under Article 22(5).
Once the detenu demands copies of the documents and statements relied upon in the grounds of detention, the detaining authority is duty-bound to furnish them with reasonable expedition.
respondent_arguments: No breach of Article 22(5) occurred because the non-supply of certain Urdu translations caused no prejudice to the detenu.
The untranslated documents consisted mainly of statements of account with English figures, some English words in capital letters, and some words in Hindi and Gujarati.

The record indicates that the detenu knows English figures, understands English words in capital letters, and can converse in Hindi and Gujarati, and was therefore not hampered in making an effective representation.

cases.principle: The detaining authority is required to supply the grounds of detention along with copies of all documents, statements, and other materials relied upon, and any unjustified delay in doing so constitutes a breach of the constitutional and legislative mandate.

Confirmed the principle that the detaining authority is required to supply the grounds of detention along with copies of all documents, statements, and other materials relied upon, and any unjustified delay in doing so constitutes a breach of the constitutional and legislative mandate.

Cited in reference to the failure of the detaining authority to supply the grounds of detention and the documents relied upon to the detenu.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, the 'grounds' for detention that must be communicated to a detenu are not merely the conclusions of fact, but all the basic facts and materials that influenced the detaining authority's decision. This requires that copies of all documents, statements, and other materials referred to in the grounds must be supplied to the detenu, and a failure to do so constitutes a breach of the constitutional mandate which vitiates the order of detention.
obiter: Where a previous detention order has been vitiated on a specific ground, greater vigilance and expedition is expected from the detaining authority in subsequent proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the continued detention of the petitioner was illegal because the subsequent failure of the detaining authority to supply the Urdu translations of the grounds and documents relied upon, after a demand was made, was a clear violation of the constitutional mandate of Article 22(5). This failure vitiates the order of detention as it prevents the detenu from making an effective representation.
legal_tests_applied: The expression 'grounds' in the context of Article 22(5) means 'nothing less than all the basic facts and materials which influenced the detaining authority in making the order of detention,' which must be communicated to the detenu.

Once a demand is made by the detenu for copies of statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention, it is the duty of the detaining authority to furnish them with reasonable expedition.

The detaining authority cannot decline to furnish copies of relied-upon documents on the ground that the grounds of detention were already sufficiently detailed to enable the petitioner to make an effective representation.
policy_considerations: When a previous detention order has been vitiated on the very same ground (failure to supply translations), greater vigilance and expedition is expected from the detaining authority in a subsequent detention.

The right to receive copies of all relied-upon documents is a necessary implication of the constitutional right to make an effective representation under Article 22(5), which is a crucial safeguard for the detenu.
